1 Discrete models Central takeaways: Strong law (expectation) pricing is subjectively fair w.r.t. beliefs, while risk-free arbitrarge pricing is objective. Teaser: forward contracts A forward contract at price \(K\) allows the holder to buy an asset at a specified price at a future time for price \(K\). Assuming interest rate \(r\) so that cash grows as \(e^{rt}\), let \(\mathbf S_t\) denote the price of the asset at time \(t\) Remark (strong law pricing). Using expectation calculus, the rational forward price is \(\mathbb{E}[S_t]\). For a greater forward price, we can sell the contract and buy the asset. For a lower forward price, we can buy the contract and sell the asset. Remark (risk-free arbitrarge pricing). However, we claim that the forward price is \(S_0 e^{rt}\). For greater forward price \(K\), we lend \(S_0\) to buy the asset right now, sell a contract, and deliver the asset at time \(t\), using the proceeds \(K\) to pay the loan \(S_0e^{rt}\), gaining \(K-S_0e^{rt}\). Net: short contract, long stock, short cash. For lower forward price \(K\), we borrow a stock, sell it immediately for \(S_0\), and buy a contract right now. At time \(t\), we buy the stock for \(K\) to pay off the loan, gaining \(S_0e^{rt} - K\). Note that there are three parties: us, contract counterparty, and stock counterparty. Payoffs below are given at time \(t\). Party \(K>S_0e^{rt}\) \(K<S_0e^{rt}\) Me stock, cash, contract. Payoff: \(K-S_0e^{rt}>0\) stock, cash, contract. Payoff: \(S_0e^{rt}-K>0\). Stock cpty stock. Payoff: \(S_0e^{rt}-S_t\) stock. Payoff: \(S_t-S_0e^{rt}\) Contract cpty contract. Payoff: \(K-S_t\) contract. Payoff: \(S_t-K\) A few salient points: The arbitrarge party is risk-free. The net loss \(-|K-S_0e^{rt}|\) is always split between the stock and contract counterparties. This does not contradict the fact that strong law pricing is fair in expectation if \(K=\mathbb{E}[S_t]\). Suppose \(\mathbb{E}[S_t]>S_0e^{rt}\) (for example, for risk premium), and that this is known by the contract counterparty. They will short the contract at \(K=S_0e^{rt}\), and the stock counterparty will lose in expectation. Suppose \(\mathbb{E}[S_t]<S_0e^{rt}\) and that this is known by the contract counterparty, they will long the contract and gain \(K-S_0e^{rt}>0\). The stock counterparty will lose in expectation. Assuming rational behavior, trade only happens when stock and contract counterparties disagree on the relative size of \(\mathbb{E}[S_t]\) compared to \(K\)). Binomial branch model Assume a simple model where: Stock has price \(s_1\) at \(t=0\), and at \(t=1\) goes up to \(\mathbf S_1=s_3\) w.p. \(p\) or down to \(\mathbf S_2=s_2\) w.p. \(\bar p\). Compound interest rate \(r\). Question: is it possible to construct a portfolio that pays \(f(3)\) when \(\mathbf S_1=s_3\) and \(f(2)\) when \(\mathbf S_2=s_2\)? Consider a portfolio \(\phi\) of stocks and \(\psi\) of cash worth \(\phi s_1 + \psi\) at the beginning. At \(t=1\), the portfolio is worth \(\phi s_3 + \psi e^{r}\) if \(\mathbf S_1=s_3\) and \(\phi s_2 + \psi e^{r}\) if \(\mathbf S_2=s_2\). Solve for the following system of equations, non-degenerate when stock is different from bond. \[ \begin{cases} \phi s_2 + \psi e^{r} = f(2) \\ \phi s_3 + \psi e^{r} = f(3) \end{cases} \] This yields the fair price (at \(t=0\))\(V=s_1\phi^*+\psi^*\) of the derivative with payoff \(f\). \[ V = e^{-r}(\bar q f_2 + q f_3), \quad q = \dfrac{s_1 e^{rt} - s_2}{s_3 - s_2}. \] Looking at \(q\), w.l.o.g. assume \(s_3>s_2\). This suggests that the risk-free strike price \(V\) is a discounted expectation w.r.t. some measure \(q\), of its possible payoffs. Note that the measure \(q\) is not the same as the probability \(p\) of the realizations. For \(q\leq 0\), we have \(s_3>s_2>s_1e^{rt}\). This means that the stock strictly dominates cash (even in the worst payoff). For \(q\geq 1\), rearranging yields \(s_1 e^r \geq s_3>s_2\), making cash dominate the stock. Binomial tree model Stock price starts at \(s_1\) at \(t=0\). If the stock price \(\mathbf S_t=s_j\), then \(\mathbf S_{t+1}\) is \(s_{2j+1}\) w.p. \(p_j\) or \(s_{2j}\) w.p. \(\bar p_j\). The cash bond has, for simplicity, constant interest rate \(r\). Note that in the tree model, the node index \(j\) is bijective with the root-to-node path. Thus, a derivative that specifies price at each node is equivalent to a derivative that specifies price for each path. Remark (risk-neutral pricing for tree model). Use backward induction to price the tree-model derivative: the value assigned to each node effectively says: “if I have this much money at this node, I can construct a portfolio that replicates the derivative payoffs which starts at this node”. Some preliminary definitions for the binomial representation theorem: The set of stock values, and the set of paths, is a process \(S\). The set of probabilities is a measure \(\mathbb P\) or \(\mathbb Q\). A filtration \((\mathcal F_j)\) is the history of the process up to time \(j\) (ordered list of visited nodes). A claim \(X\) on the tree is a function of the filtration at some time horizon \(T\); it assigns a claim value to each path. Denote the conditional expectation operator \(\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}(\cdot\, | \mathcal F_j)\). A previsible process \(\phi\) is a process whose value at any given node at tick \(j\) is only dependent upon its history up to that point. Definition 1.1 (martingale) A process \(S\) is a martingale w.r.t. \(\mathbb P\) and filtration \((\mathcal F_j)\) if \[ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}(S_k|\mathcal F_j) = S_j, \quad \forall j\leq k \] In other words, the future EV of the process under \(\mathbb P\), conditional on its history up to time \(j\), is equal to the process’s value at time \(j\). One salient example of a martingale: Proposition 1.1 (conditional expectation extension) For any claim \(X\) and measure \(\mathbb P\), the process \(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}(X|\mathcal F_j)\) is a martingale. Proof: Simply note that for \(k\geq j\), by the law of total expectation, we have \[ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P} \left[ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}(X|\mathcal F_k) \big| \mathcal F_j \right] = \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}(X|\mathcal F_j) \] Theorem 1.1 (binomial representation theorem) Suppose there exists \(\mathbb Q\) such that the binomial price process \(S\) is a \(\mathbb Q\)-martingale. Then, for any other \(\mathbb Q\)-martingale \(N\), there exists a previsible process \(\phi\) such that \[ N_j = N_0 + \sum_{k=1}^j \phi_k \Delta S_k \] where \(\Delta S_k = S_k - S_{k-1}\) and \(\phi_j\) is the value of \(\phi\) at the appropriate node at time \(j\). Note that \(N_0\) is a fixed value, and that based on the definition of \(\Delta S\), the process value \(\phi_k\) is computable at time \(k-1\). In other words, any \(\mathbb Q\)-martingale is equivalent (up to constant) to the accumulation of a previsible adjusting process (this would inform our purchase of the stock), times the stock price change, if the stock price is a \(\mathbb Q\)-martingale. \(\phi_k\) provides for the degrees of freedom to adjust the magnitude of the process changes in a previsible manner, and there is no price-dependent term due to the martingale property. The martingale property eliminates the price-dependent “constant” degrees of freedom, leaving only the previsible, scaling degrees of freedom which are only dependent upon the price change. The scaling process \(\phi\) denotes the previsible stock allocation. Proof: For the simple \(2\)-branch case, denote \(s_{\mathrm{now}}, s_{\mathrm{up}}, s_{\mathrm{down}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{now}}, n_{\mathrm{up}}, n_{\mathrm{down}}\), solve for \[ n_{\mathrm{up}} = N_0 + \phi_1 (s_{\mathrm{up}} - s_{\mathrm{now}}), \quad n_{\mathrm{down}} = N_0 + \phi_1 (s_{\mathrm{down}} - s_{\mathrm{now}}) \] The scaling \(\phi_1\) will be \((n_{\mathrm{up}} - n_{\mathrm{down}}) / (s_{\mathrm{up}} - s_{\mathrm{down}})\). Inductively, consider \[ \Delta N_j = \phi_j \Delta S_j + k \] where \(\phi_j\) is the ratio of the up-down difference of \(N\) versus \(S\) at the node under consideration at time \(j\). Next, take the expectation of both sides and use the martingale property \[ \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} \left[ \Delta N_j \big| \mathcal F_{j-1} \right]_{=0} = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} \left[ \phi_j \Delta S_j\big| \mathcal F_{j-1} \right]_{=0} + k \implies k = 0 \] Binomial tree pricing Assume in full generality a stock process \(S\) and a bond process \(B\) (with \(B_0=1\)). Fixing claim \(X\) and time horizon \(T\): First, annul the time growth of money: define the discounted claim \(B_T^{-1}X\) and the discounted stock process \(Z_j=(B_j^{-1}S_j)\). Assumption : in a sensible world, there is a measure \(\mathbb Q\) such that the discounted stock process \(Z_j\) is a \(\mathbb Q\)-martingale (see discussion in branch case). This is known as the fundamental theorem of asset pricing and provable by the separating hyperplane theorem, which introduces the existence of a positive linear functional. Extend the discounted claim \(B_T^{-1}X\) to a \(\mathbb Q\)-martingale \(E\) (proposition 1.1). Write \(E_j = E_0 + \sum_{k=1}^j \phi_k \Delta Z_k\) by theorem 1.1. Here \(E_0 = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}(B_T^{-1}X) = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}(E)\). Construction as follows: at time \(j\), but portfolio \(\Pi_j\) consisting of \(\phi_{j+1}\) units of stock and \(\psi_{j+1} = E_j - \phi_{j+1} Z_j\) units of cash. At time \(0\), \(\Pi_0\) is worth \(\phi_1 S_0 + \psi_1 = E_0\). The value of \(\Pi_{\forall j}\) (from the POV of \(t=0\)) is always \(E_j\). At time \(1\), \(\Pi_0\) is worth \(\phi_1 S_1 + \psi_1 = E_0 + \phi_1 \Delta Z_1 = E_1\). This is enough to finance \(\Pi_1\). The strategy \((\psi, \phi)\) defined as such is self-financing, in that holding \(\Pi_t\) from \(t\mapsto t+1\) is sufficient to finance \(\Pi_{t+1}\). Theorem 1.2 (claim pricing formula) By the risk-free construction, the value at tick-time \(j\) of a claim \(X\) maturing at some time \(T\) is \[ \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\left[ (B_j B_T^{-1}) X \big| \mathcal F_j \right] \] In other words, it is the conditional expectation of the cash-discounted claim w.r.t. the martingale measure \(\mathbb Q\) for the underlying. The value above is observed at time \(j\). Note that \(B_j B_T^{-1}\) is the normalized discount factor w.r.t. this value observation. Example 1.1 (trivial example) Consider cash without interest and a stock priced at \(1\). At the end, the stock is worth either \(2\) or \(0.5\). What is the worth of a bet which pays \(1\) if the stock goes up? The ratio of (the up-down difference of the claim) to (the up-down difference of the stock) is \(1/(3/2)=2/3\). To fulfill the claim when the stock goes up, we need to hold \(1 - 2/3\cdot 2 = -1/3\) of cash. Thet net portfolio is then \((-1/3, 2/3)\) of cash and stock, worth \(1/3\) at the beginning.

2 Continuous models Preliminaries Definition 2.1 (stochastic process) Given a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal F, \mathbb P)\), where \(\Omega\) is the sample space. \(\mathcal F\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra of events to which probabilities can be assigned. \(\mathbb P\) is a probability measure on \(\mathcal F\). A random variable is a measurable function \(X: \Omega 	o \mathbb R\). The \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by \(X\) is \(\sigma(X) = \{X^{-1}(B) \mid B\in \mathbb B(\mathbb R)\}\subseteq\mathcal F\); it encodes the information about \(\Omega\) that’s revealable by \(X\); definition extends naturally to vector-valued random variables (or collection of random variables). \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are independent if \(\sigma(X_1), \dots, \sigma(X_n)\) are independent: \[ P(\{X_j\in A_j\}) = \prod_{j=1}^n P(X_j\in A_j) \] Independence of random variables are defined analogously. Let \(T\subseteq \mathbb R_+\) be the time index; a real-valued stochastic process is a measurable map \[ X: \Omega 	imes T 	o \mathbb R. \] so that \(X_{ orall t\in T}\) is a random variable. A filtration \((\mathcal F_{t\in T})\) is an increasing family of \(\sigma\)-algebras satisfying \(\mathcal F_0\subseteq \mathcal F_{0\leq s\leq t}\subseteq \mathcal F_t\subseteq \mathcal F\). Definition 2.2 (filtration and processes) The natural filtration of a stochastic process \(X\) is the filtration \((\mathcal F_t)\) defined by \[ \mathcal F_t = \sigma(X_s \mid s\leq t). \] A stochastic process is adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)\) if \(X_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable for all \(t\in T\); this asks that the value of \(X_t\) is uniquely determined by distinguishable sample partitions known up to time \(t\). Brownian process By intuition, a continuous process should be continuous, variable across time, and real-valued. Example 2.1 (tentative random walk) Given a positive integer \(n\), define the binomial process \(W_n(t)\) with \(W_n(0) = 0\). Layer spacing \(\delta = 1/n\). Up and down jumps with equal size \(1/\sqrt n\). Measure \(\mathbb P\) uniform between up and down jumps. In other words, given a sequence of i.i.d. \(X_j\) with \(\pm 1\), define \[ W_n\left(\dfrac j night) = W_n\left(\dfrac{j-1} night) + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt n} X_j \] The definition of \(W_n(1)\) is (second argument denoting standard deviation): \[ W_n(t) = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{nt} X_j}{\sqrt n}\sim \mathcal N\left( 0, \sqrt t ight) \] Future movements away from a position are independent of the history up to that point. \(W_n(s+t)-W_n(s)\sim \mathcal N(0, \sqrt t)\). Definition 2.3 (Brownian process) A process \((W_{t\geq 0})\) is a \(\mathbb P\)-Brownian process iff \(W_t\) is continuous with \(W_0=0\). Under \(\mathbb P\), the random variable \(W_t\sim \mathcal N(0, t)\). The increment \(W_{s+t} - W_s\sim \mathcal N(0, t)\) under \(\mathcal P\) and is independent of \(\mathcal F_s\). An exponential Brownian process is defined by \(X_t = \exp(\sigma W_t + \mu t)\). Definition 2.4 (standard Brownian process) The standard Brownian process (also known as the Wiener process) consists of the following components: Sample space \(\Omega\) : \(C_0([0, \infty)	o \mathbb R)\) \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the uniform topology; makes “evaluate the path at finitely many points” measurable. Probability measure \(\mathbb P:\Omega	o [0, 1]\) given by the Wiener measure (see 2.7). Process : \(W_t(\omega) = \omega(t)\) for all \(t\geq 0\). It is simply the coordinate map; the standard Brownian process \(W_t\) is canonical due to the canonical coordinate-map process. Remark. A Brownian process is a process-measure pair! Alternative Brownian processs might exist (see CMG theorem)! A standard Brownian process with previsible drift \(W_t+\mu_t\) is not Brownian under the Wiener measure, but is Brownian under a tilted measure. Stochastic calculus Recall the classical, Newtonian differential notations: If \(f_t\) and \(	ilde f_t\) are differentiable, agreeing at \(0\), and \(df_t = d	ilde f_t\) (here \(df_t\) overloads for the derivative function), then \(f_t = 	ilde f_t\). Given differentiable \(f\), there is a unique drift \(\mu_t\) such that \(f_t = f_0 + \int_0^t \mu_s\, ds\) for all \(t\). Remark. The differential notation \(df = \mu(f, t)\, dt\) is a recipe for building differentiable functions from a drift function. Intuition: differentiable functions zoom to tangent lines, while Brownian process zooms to Brownian process; this inspires the following definition: Definition 2.5 (continuous Itô processes, diffusion) A stochastic process (more restrictive definition) \(X_t\) is a continuous process such that \[ egin{align} dX_t &= \sigma_t\, dW_t + \mu_t\, dt \ X_t &= X_0 + \int_0^t \sigma_s\, dW_s + \int_0^t \mu_s\, ds \end{align}\] where \(\sigma, \mu\) are \(\mathcal F\)-previsible processes such that \(\int_0^t (\sigma_s^2 + |\mu_s|)\, ds < \infty\) a.s. When \(\sigma, \mu\) are only dependent on \(X_t\) (instead of the full history), every strong solution is a diffusion. Remark (justification for Brownian process as fundamental building block). Brownian process is the continuous limit of equi-probable binary branching processes. Any “reasonable” branching can be approximated by an affine transformation of such branching, with offset and scale given by \(\mu_t\) and \(\sigma_t\), respectively. Change of process measure Define by \(\zeta_t\) the Radon-Nikodym derivative taken up to the horizon \(t\): i.e. it is the likelihood-ratio map measurable by \(\mathcal F_t\). Fixing a horizon \(T\) and calculate the Radon-Nikodym derivative \(d\mathbb Q/d\mathbb P\) at time \(T\), we have \[ \zeta_t = \mathbb E_{\mathbb P} \left[ \dfrac{d\mathbb Q}{d\mathbb P}  igg| \mathcal F_t ight], \quad  orall t\leq T \] Remark. The expectation above w.r.t. \(\mathcal F_t\) makes sure that \(\zeta_t\) is adapted to the information available up to time \(t\) only. In the discrete picture, this expectation equivalently puts a unique value on each node at time \(t\). The expectation is taken w.r.t. \(\mathbb P\) because \(\mathbb Q\) is in the numerator (so conditionals sum to \(1\)), while conditionals in \(\mathbb P\) are in the denominator. See example below. Example 2.4 (simple illustration) Consider two 2-level binary-tree processes \(\mathbb Q, \mathbb P\) with the first level parameterized by \(q_1\), the second by \(q_2, q_3\) respectively; same for \(p\). Under \(\mathbb Q\), the tail probabilities are \(q_1q_2, q_1 ar{q_2},  ar{q_1}q_3,  ar{q_1} ar{q_3}\). Same for \(p\). We have \(\zeta_2 = \left(\dfrac{q_1q_2}{p_1p_2}, \dfrac{q_1 ar{q_2}}{p_1 ar{p_2}}, \dfrac{ ar{q_1}q_3}{ ar{p_1}p_3}, \dfrac{ ar{q_1} ar{q_3}}{ ar{p_1} ar{p_3}}ight)\) and \(\zeta_1 = \left(\dfrac{q_1}{p_1}, \dfrac{ ar{q_1}}{ ar{p_1}}ight)\). Think as: \(\zeta_t X_t\) under \(\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\) converts the transition probabilities in \([0, t]\) to measure \(\mathbb Q\), but we over-compensated on the transition in \([0, s]\) since we’ve already conditioned on \(\mathcal F_s\). 3 Options Pricing Salient takeaways: Two approaches to the Black-Scholes equation: they are related by the Feynmann-Kac conditions. Martingales: Preliminaries Definition 3.1 (portfolio) A (stock-bond) portfolio is a pair \((\phi_t, \psi_t)\) of real-valued processes. The security component \(\phi\) should be \(\mathcal F\)-previsible. A portfolio is self-financing if \[ dV_t = \phi_t\, dS_t + \psi_t\, dB_t \] Note that the value of the portfolio is \[ V_t = \phi_t\, S_t + \psi_t\, B_t \] The self-financing equation is non-trivial (trivial only when \(\phi, \psi\) are constant), else the time-derivatives of the product rules must cancel out. Note that left-continuous (left-limit approaches correctly) \(\phi_t(\forall \omega)\) is previsible. Example 3.1 (non-trivial self-financing strategy) Consider \((\phi_t = 2W_t, \psi_t = -t - W_t^2)\). Here we hold double the stock price’s amount of shares, and short \(t+W_t^2\) amount of cash. Calculating \(V_t = 2W_t^2 - W_t^2 - t = W_t^2 - t\) and checking the SDE: \[\begin{align} dV_t &= d(W_t^2 - t) = 2W_t\, dW_t \\ \phi_t\, dW_t + (\psi_t\, dB_t)_{=0} &= 2W_t\, dW_t \end{align}\] Definition 3.2 (replicating strategy) A replicating strategy for a claim \(X\) which depends up to time \(T\) is a self-financing portfolio \((\phi, \psi)\) such that \(\|\sigma\phi\|_{T, 2} < \infty\) and \(V_t = \phi_tS_t + \psi_T B_t = X\). Black-Scholes Definition 3.3 (Black-Scholes model) Assuming deterministic \(r, \mu, \sigma\) such that the bond price \(B_t\) and stock price \(S_t\) follows \[ B_t = e^{rt}, \quad S_t = S_0 \exp(\sigma W_t + \mu t) \] Zero rates For simplicity, first assume that \(r=0\). The three steps to replication are: Find a risk-free measure \(\mathbb Q\) under which \(S_t\) is a martingale. Form the claim process \(E_t = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[X|\mathcal F_t]\). Find a previsible process such that \(dE_t = \phi_t\, dS_t\). Then \(\phi_t\) is the stock holding. For step 1, construct the SDE using Ito (definition 2.6): \[\begin{align} dS_t &= S_t \left[\sigma\, dW_t + \left(\mu + \dfrac {\sigma^2} 2\right)\, dt\right] \end{align}\] Next, kill the \((\mu + \sigma^2/2)/\sigma\) drift by shifting to a \(\mathbb Q\)-measure using CMG theorem 2.1 under which \((\mathbb P, W_t)\mapsto (\mathbb Q, \tilde W_t=W_t + (\mu/\sigma + \sigma/2)t)\) and \[ dS_t = \sigma S_t\, d \tilde W_t \] Then \(S_t\) is a martingale under theorem 2.4. For steps \(2\) and \(3\), form the martingale claim process \(E_t\) and invoke the martingale representation theorem to obtain \(dE_t = \phi_t\, dS_t\). Consider the portfolio \[ \left(\phi_t, \psi_t = E_t - \phi_t S_t \right) \] Note that for \(r=0\), we have \(B_t=1\) so \(V_t = \phi_t S_t + \psi_t B_t = E_t\), so \(dV_t = dE_t = \phi_t\, dS_t\) by construction in step \(3\), so the portfolio is self-financing. Under the exponential-Brownian assumption, \(\mathbb Q=\mathbb P\iff \mu = -\dfrac 1 2 \sigma^2\). Substituting \(\sigma \tilde W_t = \sigma W_t + (\mu + \sigma^2/2) t\), we find that \(S_t\) is tractable under the new measure: \[ S_t = S_0 \exp \left( \sigma \tilde W_t - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2} t \right) \] Non-zero rates Consider constant, nonzero rates \(r\). Form a discounted stock \(Z_t = B_t^{-1} S_t\) and discounted claim \(B_T^{-1}X\). These values are discounted w.r.t. \(t=0\). Then \[\begin{align} Z_t &= S_0 \exp \left[ \sigma W_t + (\mu - r) t \right] \\ dZ_t &= Z_t \left[ \sigma\, dW_t + \left(\mu - r + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)\, dt \right] \end{align}\] In short, \((S_t, \mu)\mapsto (Z_t, \mu - r)\). The new martingale measure \(\mathbb Q\) is formed analogously. Similarly construct \(E_t = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[B_T^{-1}X \mid \mathcal F_t]\) and use the martingale representation theorem to form \(dE_t = \phi_t\, dZ_t\). Let’s assess holding \(\phi_t, \psi_t=E_t - \phi_t Z_t\) (stock, bond) in the real world. Note that bond holding is calculated based on discounted stock \(Z_t\), not original stock. Value process \(V_t = \phi_t S_t + (E_t - \phi_t B_t^{-1} S_t) B_t = E_t\, B_t \implies dV_t = B_t \, dE_t + E_t\, dB_t\) Product rule follows from the zero-volatility assumption for the \(B_t\) process. On the other hand, note that \(dS_t = d(B_tZ_t)\) and \(\phi_t\, dZ_t = dE_t\) to match: \[\begin{align} \phi_t\, dS_t + \psi_t\, dB_t &= \phi_t\, dS_t + E_t\, dB_t - \phi_t Z_t\, dB_t \\ &= \phi_t B_t\, dZ_t + \phi_t Z_t\, dB_t + E_t\, dB_t - \phi_t Z_t\, dB_t \\ &= B_t\, dE_t + E_t\, dB_t = dV_t \end{align}\] Details of the discount process: The martingale construction \(dE_t = \phi_t\, dZ_t\) says that changes in the discounted claim’s value should be equivalent to changes in the discounted stock’s value. Both are discounted. From \(V_t=E_tB_t\), changes in the portfolio price (which is the undiscounted \(\mathbb Q\)-value of the claim measured at time \(t\) is due to two pieces: \(B_t\, dE_t\) (change in discounted value). \(E_t\, dB_t\) (interest rate effect). From a holdings perspective, changes in the stock price \(\phi_t\, dS_t\) contributes a \(B_t\, dE_t\) term (desired) and a \(\phi_t Z_t\, dB_t\) term which counteracts the relevant term in cash holding value difference. Theorem 3.1 (Black-Scholes pricing) Under Black-Scholes assumptions for prices and interest rates, all integrable claims \(X\) at horizon \(T\) have replicating strategies with arbitrage price (at time \(t\)): \[ V_t = B_t \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[B_T^{-1}X \mid \mathcal F_t] = e^{-r(T-t)} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[X\mid \mathcal F_t] \] where \(\mathbb Q\) is the martingale measure for the discounted stock \(B_t^{-1}S_t\). Proposition 3.1 (European call) Consider the call option payout \(X(S_T) = (S_T-k)^+\). \[ V = e^{-rT} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} (S_T-k)^+ \] Proceeding to calculation, recall that \[\begin{align} d Z_t &= Z_t \left[ \sigma\, dW_t + \left(\mu - r + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)\, dt \right] = \sigma Z_t \, d\tilde W_t \\ \sigma\, dW_t &= \sigma\, d\tilde W_t - \left(\mu - r + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)\, dt \\ d\log S_t &= \sigma\, dW_t + \mu\, dt = \sigma\, d\tilde W_t + \left(r - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)\, dt \end{align}\] Under the martingale measure \(\mathbb Q\), \(\log S_t\sim \mathcal N((r-\sigma^2/2)t, \sigma^2)\). The greater the volatility, the lower the drift. Fix horizon \(T\) and introduce \(Z\sim \mathcal N(-\sigma^2t/2, \sigma^2)\), we have \[\begin{align} V &= e^{-rT} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} (S_T-k)^+ \\ &= e^{-rT} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} (S_0 e^{Z+rT}-k)^+ = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} (S_0 e^{Z}-k e^{-rT})^+ \end{align}\] Final words Remark. To price an instrument with exercising optionality: suppose the claim purchaser has a set of options \(A\) and receives payoff \(X_a\) at time \(T(a)\), the issuer should charge \[ V = \sup_{a\in A} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[B_{T(a)}^{-1} X_a] \] Although the martingale representation theorem does not explicitly provide \(\phi_t\), we can use \(dE_t = \phi_t\, dS_t\implies \phi_t = \partial_{S} E {\big|}_t\). Proposition 3.2 (terminal value pricing) Let \(X=f(S_T)\). Denote the value of derivative at time \(t\) by \[ V_t(s_t)=V(S_t, t) = B_t \,\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} \left[ B_T^{-1} f(S_T) \mid S_t =s_t \right] \] The trading strategy is given by \(\phi_t = \partial_{S_t} V_t {\big|}_{s_t, t}\). This amount of stock holdings correctly equates the change in replicating portfolio price relative to stock price change Recall that \(\sigma\, dW_t = \sigma\, d\tilde W_t + \dots\), then \(S_t = e^{\sigma W_t + \mu t}\) implies the SDE form \[ dS_t = S_t \left[ \sigma \, dW_t + \left(\mu + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\right) t \right] = S_t (\sigma\, d\tilde W_t + r\, dt) \] Directly applying Ito \(V(S_t, t)\) yields (here derivatives are taken w.r.t. \(S_t=s_t\)) the SDE: \[\begin{align} dV_t &= \left( \sigma S_t\, \partial_{S} V \right)\, d\tilde W_t + \left( \dfrac{\sigma^2 S_t^2}{2} \partial_S^2 V + r S_t\, \partial_{S} V + \partial_{t} V \right)\, dt \end{align}\] On the other hand, using the self-financing condition yields \[\begin{align} dV_t &= \phi_t\, dS_t + \psi_t\, (dB_t)_{=rB_t\, dt} \\ &= (\sigma S_t \phi_t)\, d\tilde W_t + (rS_t\phi_t + r\psi_tB_t)\, dt \\ &= (\sigma S_t \phi_t)\, d\tilde W_t + rV_t\, dt \end{align}\] Matching the volatility terms yield \(\phi_t = \partial_{S} V\). Matching the drift terms yield \[ \dfrac{\sigma^2 S_t^2}{2} \partial_S^2 V + rS_t \, \partial_{S} V - r V + \partial_{t} V = 0 \] Coupling with the boundary condition \(V(s, T)=f(s)\) yields the pricing equation. Remark (miscellany). If an option is out of the money, both bond and stock holdings go to zerl. When option approaches expiration in-the-money, stock holding goes to \(1\) and bond to \(-k\).

4 Pricing examples Foreign exchange Definition 4.1 (Black-Scholes currency model) Consider the dollar cash bond \(B_t\), its sterling counterpart \(D_t\), and the dollar worth \(C_t\) of one pound. We assume \[ B_t = e^{rt}, \quad D_t = e^{ut} \] \[ C_t = C_0 \exp(\sigma W_t + \mu t) \] How should we price a claim \(X\) denominated in pound units? Intuition: the \(S_tD_t\), the dollar price of the pound bond, is a stock-like tradable. Pricing proceeds by identifying the discounted pound process, zeroing the drift, and identifying \(C_t\) under the risk-neutral measure \(\mathbb Q\): \[\begin{align} Z_t &= B_t^{-1} D_t C_t \\ &= C_0 \exp \left( \sigma W_t + (\mu + u - r)t \right) \\ dZ_t &= Z_t \left[ \sigma\, dW_t + \left( \mu + u - r + \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2} \right)\, dt \right] = Z_t \sigma d\tilde W_t \\ Z_t &= C_0 \exp \left( \sigma \tilde W_t - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\, t \right) \end{align}\] Define the discounted claim \(E_t = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}(B_T^{-1} X\mid \mathcal F_t)\) and use martingale representation to obtain \(dE_t = \phi_t\, dZ_t\). Definition 4.2 (FX claim pricing) Claims in foreign currency have arbitrage value \[ V_t = B_t \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[B_T^{-1} X\mid \mathcal F_t] \] where \(\mathbb Q\) is the martingale measure for \(Z_t\). Example 4.1 (forward contract) Consider the forward contract payoff \(X=C_t-k\): calculate \[ V_t = e^{-r(T-t)} \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[C_T - k\mid \mathcal F_t] \] Let’s first determine the arbitrage strike \(k\): recalling \(C_t = Z_t B_t D_t^{-1}\) yields (arbitrage price means that value of claim at expiry is \(0\)): \[\begin{align} k&=\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[C_T\mid \mathcal F_T] = C_0 \, \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q} \exp\left[ \sigma \tilde W_T + \left( r - u - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{2} \right) T \right] = C_0 e^{(r-u)T} \end{align}\] Note that \(\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[C_T\mid \mathcal F_t] = e^{(r-u)(T-t)} C_t\) since \(C_t=Z_tB_tD_t^{-1}\) carries drift. Under this strike, the contract’s price at time \(t\) is \[\begin{align} V_t &= e^{-r(T-t)}\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[C_T - C_0 e^{(r-u)T} \mid \mathcal F_t] \\ &= \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[e^{rt - rT} e^{(r-u)(T-t)} C_t - C_0 e^{rt - uT} \mid \mathcal F_t] \\ &= e^{-uT}\left( e^{ut} C_t - e^{rt}C_0 \right) \end{align}\] To obtain the portfolio, calculate the discounted value and calculate \(dE_t / dZ_t = e^{-uT}\): this is the amount of pound sterling needed to replicate the claim. \[\begin{align} E_t &= B_t^{-1}V_t = e^{-uT}(e^{(u-r)t} C_t - C_0) = e^{-uT}(Z_t - Z_0) \end{align}\] The dollar cash position is \(E_t = \phi_t Z_t = -e^{-uT}C_0\).
5 Interest rates Bond basics Simple rate model

5 Interest rates Bond basics Definition 5.1 (discount bond) A discount bond is a promise to pay \(1\) dollar at time \(T\) for a discounted price \(P(0, T)\), so \(P(T, T)=1\). The market price is denoted \(P(t, T)\). Bond prices is a two-dimensional surface. The more distant the payment maturity, less current worth. Boundary condition \(P(\forall T, T)=1\). Definition 5.2 (yield) Given current price \(P(t, T)\), its compounded price at \(T=t\) is (assuming constant compounding) \[ P(T, T) = 1 = e^{R(t, T)(T-t)}P(t, T)\implies R(t, T) = -\dfrac{\log P(t, T)}{T-t} \] The yield \(R(t, T)\) is the implied continuous compounding rate to justify the price of the bond beginning at \(t\) and maturing at \(T\). We can recover the price by \[ P(t, T) = \exp \left[ -(T-t)R(t, T) \right] \] Assuming stable interest rates, long-term yields are generally higher. If long-term rates are expected to fall, yield curve becomes inverted. The instantaneous rate, or short rate, is the rate of borrowing money at the present at time \(t\). It is given by \[ r_1(t) = \lim_{\epsilon\to 0} R(t, t+\epsilon) = -\partial_{2} \log P(t, t) \] The short rate entails the instantaneous rate of borrowing right now, but what about the projected instantaneous rate at some future time \(T\)? Definition 5.3 (forward rate) The projected (at time \(t\)) rate of instantaneous borrowing at time \(T\) is \[ f(t, T) = -\partial_{T} \log P(t, T) \] To compute this, consider a forward contract which entails agreeing at time \(t\) to make a payment at \(T_1>t\) and receive payment at \(T_2\). To replicate the ability to fulfill this contract at \(t\), we need to buy \(T_2\) bond and short some \(k\) units of \(T_1\) bond. The current price of this portfolio is \(P(t, T_2) - kP(t, T_1)\). Setting this to \(0\) yields the arbitrage price (at reference \(t\)) \(k=P(t, T_2)/P(t, T_1)\). Then \(k=P_t(T_1, T_2)\) is the forward price of purchasing \(T_2\)-bond at \(T_1\), striked at time \(t\). The corresponding implied yield of this price is \[ R_t(T_1, T_2) = -\dfrac{\log k}{T_2-T_1} = -\dfrac{\log P(t, T_2) - \log P(t, T_1)}{T_2-T_1} \] Take \(T_2\to T_1\) to obtain the instantaneous rate. The bond price can be recovered by \[ P(t, T) = \exp \left( -\int_t^T f(t, u)\, du \right) \] The yield curve \(T\mapsto R(t, T)\) measures the cumulative effect of forward rates (e.g. yield of \(3\)-year bond cumulatively accounts for rates at \(1, 2, 3\) years. The forward rate isolates this effect. Simple rate model Definition 5.4 (simple rate model) Given an integrable forward rate curve \(f(0, T)\), the forward curve evolves as \[\begin{align} d_t f(t, T) &= \sigma\, dW_t + \alpha(t, T)\, dt \\ f(t, T) &= \sigma W_t + f(0, T) + \int_0^t \alpha(s, T)\, ds \end{align}\] Here we ask \(\alpha\) to be a bounded, deterministic function. Fixing \(t\), forward rates at different maturities are deterministic \[ f(t, S) - f(t, T) = \int_0^t \alpha(s, S) - \alpha(s, T)\, ds \] Differences throughout time: all bonds share the same random source of movement \(\sigma W_{\delta t}\). \[\begin{align} f(t_1, S) - f(t_0, S) &= \sigma (W_{t_1} - W_{t_0}) + \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \alpha(s, S)\, dS \end{align}\] Let’s consider two tradable securities: Numeraire: cash bond formed by the instantaneous rate \(r_t\): \[ dB_t = r_t B_t\, dt, \quad B_0 = 1 \] Noting that \(r_t = f(t, T)\) yields \(r_t = \sigma W_t + f(0, t) + \int_0^t \alpha(s, t)\, ds\). Substitute \[\begin{align} B_t &= \exp \left(\int_0^t r_s\, ds\right) = \exp \left( \sigma\, \int_0^t W_s\, ds + \int_0^t f(0, s)\, ds + \int_0^t \int_0^s \alpha(u, s)\, du \, ds \right) \\ &= \exp \left( \sigma\, \int_0^t W_s\, ds + \int_0^t f(0, s)\, ds + \int_0^t \int_s^t \alpha(s, u)\, du \, ds \right) \end{align}\] Note that the last two double-integrals are equivalent by \((0\leq u\leq s\leq t)\cong (\leq s\leq u\leq t)\). For the other tradable, pick bond at price \(T\) and compute \[\begin{align} P(t, T) &= \exp \left(-\int_t^T f(t, u)\, du\right) \\ &= \exp \left[-\int_t^T \left( \sigma W_t + f(0, u) + \int_0^t \alpha(s, u)\, ds \right)\, du\right] \\ &= \exp -\left[ \sigma (T-t) W_t + \int_t^T f(0, u)\, du + \int_0^t \int_t^T \alpha(s, u)\, du\, ds \right] \end{align}\] Compute the discounted “stock” \(Z_t=B_t^{-1} P(t, T)\): \[\begin{align} -\log Z_t &= \sigma(T-t)W_t + \sigma\int_0^t W_s\, ds + \underbrace{\int_0^T f(0, s)\, ds}_{\text{constant}} + \int_0^t \int_s^T \alpha(s, u)\, du\, ds \\ d[(T-t)W_t] &= -W_t\, dt + (T-t)\, dW_t, \quad d\left[ \int_0^t W_s\, ds \right] = W_t\, dt \\ -\dfrac{dZ_t}{Z_t} &= \sigma(T-t)\, dW_t + \left[ \int_t^T \alpha(t, u)\, du - \dfrac{\sigma^2(T-t)^2}{2}\right]\, dt \end{align}\] Invoke CMG theorem to shift to a measure \(\mathbb Q\) such that \(\mathbb P\mapsto \mathbb Q\) effects \(dZ_t = -\sigma(T-t) Z_t\, d\tilde W_t\) by \[ d\tilde W_t = dW_t - \left[\dfrac{1}{\sigma(T-t)} \int_t^T \alpha(t, u)\, du - \dfrac{\sigma(T-t)}{2}\right]_{\gamma_t}\, dt \] Take any claim \(X\) expiring at time \(S\) and take the form the discounted claim process \(E_t = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}(B_S^{-1}X\mid \mathcal F_t)\) and let \(dE_t = \phi_t\, dZ_t\). Remark (replicating short-maturity bonds). Take \(X=1\) expiring at time \(S\) — this instrument corresponds to a \(S\)-bond. The claim above implies that every \(S\)-bond can be constructed from a \(T_{\geq S}\) bond and compounding cash. To prevent arbitrage, these prices must be the same. Let’s consider the implications: The discounted process \(Y_t=B_t^{-1}P(t, S)\) of the \(S\)-bond satisfies \[ -\dfrac{dY_t}{Y_t} = \sigma(S-t)\, dW_t + \left[ \int_t^S \alpha(t, u)\, du - \dfrac{\sigma^2(S-t)^2}{2}\right]\, dt \] Define the (term, time)-dependent drift function \[ (S, t)\mapsto \gamma_t^S = -\dfrac{\sigma(S-t)}{2} + \dfrac{1}{\sigma(S-t)} \int_t^S \alpha(t, u)\, du \] such that \(dY_t = -\sigma (S-t) Y_t(dW_t+\gamma_t^S\, dt)\). Equivalently using \(\mathbb Q\) for martingale-ing the \(T\)-bond, we have \[ dY_t = -\sigma(S-t)Y_t[d\tilde W_t + (\gamma_t^S - \gamma_t^T)\, dt] \] Recall that no-arbitrage implies that every tradable instrument must be driftless (martingale) under the risk-neutral measure, which means that \(\gamma_t^S = \gamma_t^T\). In particular, this implies that \(\partial_{T} \gamma_t^T = 0\). Use the definition for \(\gamma_t^T\) and differentiate upon multiplying both sides by \(\sigma(T-t)\) to obtain \[\begin{align} \sigma \gamma_t^T &= \partial_{T} \left[\sigma(T-t) \gamma_t^T\right] \\ &= \partial_{T} \left[ -\dfrac{\sigma^2(T-t)^2}{2} + \int_t^T \alpha(t, u)\, du \right] \\ &= -\sigma^2(T-t) + \alpha(t, T) \\ \alpha(t, T) &= \sigma^2(T-t) + \sigma \gamma_t \end{align}\] Two salient takeaways: The drift is constrained to be the sum of a maturity-independent term \(\sigma\gamma_t\) plus a particular function \(\sigma^2(T-t)\). The time-dependent \(\gamma_t\) is, again the market price of risk upon recognizing, for \(\Sigma = \sigma(T-t)\). \[ \dfrac{d_t P(t, T)}{P(t, T)} = -\Sigma(t, T)\, dW_t + (r_t - \Sigma(t, T) \gamma_t)\, dt \] Models with weaker assumptions (HJM for forward rate) or equivalent characterizations (e.g. using short-rates).
